title: Crosswind Council
logline: No law on the hill covers the egg — a wish is the largest key ever cut, and Mr. BaneWAP wants it filed, appraised, and auctioned to himself.
epigraph: A key may be filed smaller in the open. It may never be grown in the dark.
description: Chapter 4 of Lore.Land: Crosswind Council. Boof carries the unspent wish to the hilltop table, where a bitter pie in a banker's crust argues it should be filed and auctioned — and the mirror shows every delegate what wanting becomes when it hoards.

content.text: Council Hill kept a great slab of split pine that refused to pick a side, and it was there, under crosswind weather, that Boof brought the egg to be argued over. She slipped beneath the trestle, chin on the timber, and found herself nose to frame with the

children.text: —an upright pane of polished weather that returned not your face but the exact shape of your wanting.

content.text: The hill smelled of two weathers at once. Round the council ring stood seven posts, and on every post an iron weathercock, rust-red at the comb. They did not follow the wind. They turned toward whatever they favoured, and the wind followed them. The crosswind was only the weathercocks disagreeing, made weather.
Twice in living memory all seven had agreed, and the hill went so still that papers stayed where they were put. Nobody remembered the vote. Everybody remembered the papers.

At the head of the slab the crosswind loom worked without a weaver: dawn-wind for the warp, squall for the weft, the shuttle flying between them on its own. It wove the council's tablecloth an inch an hour, honey-gold and squall-teal, and when the vote turned, the weave changed colour.

Cut into the slab's edge, at nose height, was the hill's first law: &[boon, bane]{table}. The founders had chiselled it in bracework before the first argument, the way a joiner writes a joint before she saws, so it could be leaned on and checked while tempers were cool. Two sides in one frame, merged without whitening either. One table round the lot, like a room you agree to stay in.

content.gloss: Two sides held in one frame, neither whitened, with a single table round the lot, like a room everyone has agreed to stay in.
content.maker: the hill's founders, before the first argument

content.text: Each delegate thumbed the braces before sitting, to be sure nobody had filed them open in the night. Nobody ever had. Boof sniffed the cut: {{cut-smell}}. The ferry delegate thumbed it last, said “Two springs, one bed,” as if that were the whole of the law, and sat.

variants: resin and a little wet wool

content.text: Above her, the law of the hill was recited as it had been recited for generations: every permission in Boon.land is a key, iron or brass, and a key may be filed smaller in the open, before witnesses, with the shavings swept into the honest jar. A key may never be grown in secret. The jar had never once been emptied, which the hill considered the point.

The Genie stood at the table's edge, hands folded, and added the one fact that mattered: a wish is the largest key ever cut. It opens the momentum of the world itself. That was when the bane-side chair creaked.

The bitter pie arrived by hired cart, lattice crust tight over berries he'd kept too long. He offered nobody a slice. The wish, he proposed, should be valued, filed, and sold to someone prepared to bear its considerable responsibilities. He paused to let the council imagine such a person. Then supplied his own name.

As the cart tipped, a berry worked loose from his lattice, plum-black with a thorn on its stem, and rolled across the pine to the youngest clerk's elbow. Boof smelled it before she saw it: cold, violet, a cellar smell, and under that something being said. On the hill they say a baneberry tells you what will go wrong, and that it goes wrong because you were told. The clerk heard, or thought he heard, that the wind would have his cap. So he took it off to keep it safe, and set it on the slab beside his chalk.

Nothing is argued on the hill until it has been written. Write it before you argue it, the founders said, and cut their own law first to show how. So while the pie was still being reasonable, the youngest clerk chalked his motion on the pine beside the law: [wish]{BaneWAP}. A window, with one man's room round it, where the law had a table. Nobody needed to raise a voice. Boof sniffed both. The law smelled of resin. The motion smelled of chalk, which comes off.

All round the ring the weathercocks swung: three to face the pie, three tails to him, the seventh spinning on its pin. The crosswind doubled, lifted the youngest clerk's cap off the slab where he had set it to keep it safe, and hung it in the gorse. Boof flattened her ears. She did not know how iron voted. She knew what it smelled like when it was cross.

content.text: The Fool’s Mirror shimmered with the fury of the split sky. It whispered in a tone like wind through eaves: "What you see is not what is, but what your wanting is becoming." The delegates looked, one by one. The boon-side saw their small wants, snug as filed keys.

Mr. BaneWAP looked longest, and the glass returned him honestly: every berry he had ever hoarded, pressed airless under crust, gone from sweet to bitter for want of being served. He was not a villain from elsewhere. He was the mirror of what wanting becomes when it stops handing out slices.
The egg, reflected beside him, showed no bidder's number and no bounding box — a wish keeps its own law, and no appraisal on the hill could get purchase on its shell.

content.text: Every court gets a vizier. I sampled that trope, folks — and honked it back as pastry.

One-footed on the unsigned auction ledger, the Fool produced a small hot hand-pie from nowhere polite — clove and windfall apple — and set it before Mr. BaneWAP with a bow. The whisperer-at-the-throne, the schemer in the sleeve — an old trope, sampled a thousand times. He returned it changed, with interest: in Boon.land the vizier is baked goods, and you can smell exactly what he's been hoarding.

img.alt: A council table under storm-light: filed keys, a coal-dark cracked egg no key covers, and a bitter pie in a banker's crust arguing for an auction.

sections.figcaption: Crosswind Council: keys narrow in the open; a wish is too large to file.

content.text: Boof watched the argument cross the pine grain like weather. Boon and bane sat under one shared squall and bargained without declaring war; that was the table's whole genius. But when the clerks brought out the rack of civic keys — iron ones honestly narrowed, brass ones watched for secret growing — not one of them matched the egg.

The youngest clerk carried the largest key to the key-file bench anyway and set it in the vise. He drew the file once, from habit, before remembering that the bench only makes keys smaller. He swept the grey filings into the honest jar and hung the key back, a hair lighter and no nearer. Blowing the last filings off his thumb, he said the register ought to have a box for what you do not know. Nobody wrote that down.

The Genie explained it the way he priced everything, flatly and without pity: a wish is not property, because it is not a thing; it is a redirection of momentum the world already has. You cannot auction a bend in the river. You can only stand where it bends.

From beneath the table, Boof could see the parts of the meeting the mirror missed: wet hems, hobnailed boots braced against the slope, {{under-table}}. Whenever a delegate struck the pine, dust shook loose beside her nose. They wanted the rain kept off their roofs and the paths kept open to their doors; some wanted more, but those wants were there beneath the grander words.

content.text: And she could see the tablecloth's hem, which showed her the vote before anyone above: teal when the bane-side spoke well, gold for the boon-side, and a muddy wet-straw weave whenever somebody spoke only to be heard. There was a good deal of wet straw.
She shifted the egg away from a drip. Above her, someone asked who would be responsible for keeping it safe.

None of the keys fitted. The oldest clerk tried the last one, set it down, and wrote: the wish stays with its finder. Round the ring the weathercocks came slowly to rest, every one pointing at the gap between the banners, which on Council Hill is how a tie is recorded. The youngest clerk wiped the pie's motion off the pine with his sleeve. “Chalk is cheaper than oak,” said a joiner on the bench, though the slab was pine.
{{rain-on-table}} on the tabletop. Across it, the pie smiled. “And who,” he asked, “inherits from the finder?” Boof's fur lifted along her back. The clerk kept his pen above the page.

content.text: Boof left the hill with the wish she had never asked to hold, down hill-slate steps dished by centuries of boots that had come down still disagreeing. Finder, the clerk had written, as if finding were a small thing a dog did with her nose and not a door the world had opened under her paws.
The Genie walked beside her, unhurried. "He will not steal it," he said of the pie on the other road. "Stealing costs a miracle. Paperwork costs pocket change, and he knows which one he can afford."

Behind them, at sundown, the clerks cut the day's end off the tablecloth and folded it for {{worst-roof}} whose roof had leaked worst that week: the one custom on the hill that has never needed a vote.

variants: the hedger at the top gate

content.text: Below the hill, two claims reached the hall of arches before supper. One named Boof. One called the wish an asset. The clerks pinned them side by side, shut the door, and went home. Under the desk, where no one thought to listen, the floor began to sing.

loreItems.description: Council law: a key may be filed smaller in the open, never grown in secret. A wish is the largest key ever cut — too large for the rack.
Mr. BaneWAP debuts: a pie of hoarded berries gone bitter in a banker's crust. He wants the wish filed, appraised, and auctioned — to himself.
The mirror chamber's truth: BaneWAP is not a foreign villain. He is the reflection of what wanting becomes when it hoards instead of serving slices.
No key covers the egg, so the council cannot rule. The wish stays with its finder. The Fool samples the evil-vizier trope and honks it back as pastry.
Council Hill's iron weathercocks vote by turning, and the crosswind is their disagreement made weather. A tie is recorded when every one of them points at the gap between the banners.

The council slab carries the hill's first law, cut in bracework before any argument: &[boon, bane]{table} — two sides, one table. Written first so it can be leaned on and checked; delegates thumb the braces before sitting to be sure nobody filed them open.

The key-file bench can only make a key smaller; its filings go into the honest jar, never emptied. The crosswind loom weaves the council's tablecloth from the hill's two winds, and the vote shows first in its hem.
At sundown the day's end of the tablecloth is cut and given to whoever's roof leaked worst that week — the one custom on the hill that has never needed a vote.

Write it before you argue it: on Council Hill a motion is chalked in braces on the pine beside the founders' law before anyone may speak to it, so the ring can see its shape while tempers are cool. Laws are cut; motions are chalked, and chalk comes off.

table.place: The top of Council Hill in crosswind weather: seven posts in a ring, an iron weathercock on each, and inside it a great slab of split pine with the hill's first law cut at nose height and worn smooth by thumbs. At the slab's head the crosswind loom weaves the tablecloth with no weaver; to one side stand the key-file bench, its vise, and an honest jar of grey filings that has never been emptied. Rain on one cheek, dust on the other, wet wool, resin — and a sourness like burnt sugar whenever the bitter pie is in session.
table.light: A split sky, warm gold sunbreak on the dawnward side and cold teal squall off the far ridge, with the table straddling the seam. The seam moves whenever the weathercocks do; if all seven ever agree, the light goes so still that papers stay where they are put.

hooks: A still afternoon. All seven weathercocks have agreed twice in living memory, and both times the hill went so still that papers stayed where they were put. Someone needs one still afternoon — to dry a harvest, to fly a lantern, to hear a whisper from the valley — and must get seven opinionated iron roosters to face the same way.

The honest jar. The jar of filings has never once been emptied, which the hill considers the point. Last night someone tried. Find out who wanted the filings, and what key they meant to grow from them in secret.

A motion for the slate. You need a permission from the hill: a ford, a mill-race, a path through a commons. Here a motion is chalked in braces on the pine before anyone may argue it, and the whole ring reads its shape before it hears a word. Write it so it holds, then argue it while tempers are cool.
encounters: The seventh weathercock spins on its pin; the crosswind doubles and hangs somebody's cap in the gorse, and the vote waits while they fetch it.
The tablecloth's hem goes the colour of wet straw under one of you. On this hill that means you are speaking only to be heard.

Under the table a delegate's pasty goes cold in a coat pocket and a twist of toffee is passed hand to hand along the bench. The hill's real wants are down here: rain off the roofs, paths open to the doors.
Rain ticks on the tabletop, then hail skips, then sleet hisses; every chalked motion on the pine begins to run, and the clerks argue whether a smudged brace still counts.
Someone looks into the Fool's Mirror and sees not their face but the exact shape of their wanting — and so does everyone standing behind them.
At sundown the clerks cut the day's end off the tablecloth and fold it for whoever's roof leaked worst that week. This week it might be one of you, and refusing is not done.

finds.use: Read its hem and you know how a vote is going before anyone says so: gold for the boon-side speaking well, teal for the bane-side, wet straw for anyone talking only to be heard. The catch: it weaves everyone at the table, you included, an inch an hour, and the cloth is kept.

File a permission smaller in the open, before witnesses, and it is honestly yours. The catch: the bench only ever makes things smaller; anything you want to grow has to be argued at the table instead, in front of the jar.

Win one over and the wind follows it; the weather on the hill leans your way for as long as it faces you. The catch: they turn toward what they favour, not toward whoever asked, and an iron rooster that has turned its tail to you does not turn back the same day.

bracework.does: The slab's own shape, borrowed: two sides of a quarrel held in one frame with one room round them. Chalk it on the pine and the shepherd and the miller can argue the ford all day without either being whitened, and neither may leave until it is settled.
bracework.costs: Chalked, it lasts until the rain. Cut, it lasts as long as the hill, and binds whoever cut it long after they have changed their mind.

table.question: All seven weathercocks have agreed twice in living memory. Nobody remembers either vote, only that the papers stayed where they were put. What did the hill agree on?
